cells.tense: You're here with it, looking closely at what's in front of you and seeing plainly what it needs.
cells.ask: Offer the next step you can hold all the way through, even if it's slower than the one you could start today
cells.core:
A garden in good hands looks like this: the beds get tended on a rhythm, the plants that needed moving got moved, and nothing out there is being fussed over that didn't ask for it. You look before you water, and the looking and the doing sit in the same motion. You can tell what's healthy from what only looks healthy, so what you feed is what's actually alive, and it keeps coming up because you keep paying attention.

That steadiness can carry more than this round. The long stretch is where it pays off — months of the same small motions, the difference showing up slowly, plenty of days when it doesn't show at all and you keep going anyway. Something real is growing here, and it can grow past the size of what you can see today.

cells.tense: You're up ahead of what's actually growing, fixing problems it hasn't shown you yet.
cells.ask: Let one person see how much you're carrying, and take the thanks they give you without waving it off
cells.core:
A garden in good hands gets handled less than people think. You look, you see, you do the one thing that's needed, and then you leave it to grow. The work sits lighter because it's aimed at what's here instead of what might turn up later, and the looking stays a pleasure instead of a job.

That's not what's happening. You inspect the shoots before they break ground and correct course for rain that hasn't shown up yet. It feels like care, but the plants get managed more than fed, and you're tired in a way rest doesn't touch. Say what you've been doing out there, plainly, to someone who'll hear it. That's what gets the weight to lift off — not another pass through the rows, and not pretending it didn't cost you.

cells.tense: You stopped looking closely a while back, and you're still standing at the spot where you set the work down.
cells.ask: Take one small thing you're owed — a hand, a rest, a turn — and let someone actually give it to you
cells.core:
A garden in good hands has someone moving through it. You can tell healthy from not, and you act on what you see, and it shows — the beds answer back, and the looking teaches you something new each season. It's not a chore you remember to do. It's how you're built to be near things that grow.

The eye is still there. You just don't use it anymore. What's growing gets left alone, and from the outside being left alone looks the same as being neglected; some of it has gone quiet, and you're not sure when that happened. Nothing needs figuring out first. Take the smallest thing you're owed from the person nearest you, and take it properly. The looking comes back when what's around you starts giving something back.

cells.tense: The careful looking is already happening — it's shaping what you do all day — and you're calling it just how you are.
cells.ask: Name one thing you do for someone that you've been calling no big deal, and say out loud that you chose it
cells.core:
A garden in good hands has someone in it who notices. You see what a thing needs and you adjust, quietly, without announcing it, and the people around you grow because of it. No one has to ask, and nothing out there feels managed — it just gets what it needs, on time, because you were paying attention.

You'd tell it as just being practical, or as what anyone would do, and that framing keeps it invisible, mostly to you. One of those choices is yours. Say it out loud as yours. Not the whole habit, just the one. It gives back something that's been doing the work with no name on it.
